claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy initially has a fine, nearly single-phase FCC matrix.
The starting alloy has clean, ductile grain boundaries with minimal pre-existing oxides or secondary-phase precipitates.
High-temperature oxidizing exposure promotes formation of predominantly Al- and Ti-rich oxides in the target alloy.
The Al- and Ti-rich oxides segregate preferentially to grain boundaries or intergranular regions.
Grain-boundary oxide formation disrupts continuity of the ductile FCC matrix.
Elevated temperature accelerates selective oxidation of Al and Ti at grain boundaries.
Oxidizing atmospheres produce a continuous or nearly continuous brittle grain-boundary oxide film.
A reducing H2/Ar atmosphere suppresses external oxidation.
Despite suppressed external oxidation, oxygen penetration in reducing atmospheres can produce localized internal oxide precipitation.
The oxide features act as stress concentrators and impede dislocation motion.
Oxide-induced weakening of intergranular cohesion ultimately causes intergranular fracture and catastrophic failure under mechanical or thermal loading.
Oxidizing exposure will produce more grain-boundary oxide decoration than the as-manufactured baseline.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce ductility and failure strain relative to the as-manufactured baseline.
Reducing exposure will produce less surface oxide but internal oxidation markers and delayed embrittlement.
Catastrophic failure will correlate with the density and connectivity of grain-boundary oxide phases.
The proposed oxidation-controlled degradation mechanism applies between 650 and 750 °C for exposure durations up to 100 hours.
Al2O3 and TiO2 are the principal candidate oxide types responsible for embrittlement.
Residual stresses from additive manufacturing may accelerate oxide formation synergistically.
